Zurich
ZOOR-ik
proper noun (a city of the Reformation)
The Swiss city (German Zürich) where Huldrych Zwingli led the first Reformed Reformation from 1519, making it a fountainhead of the Reformed tradition.

📖 Biblical Definition

Zurich was the Swiss city where Huldrych Zwingli, appointed people's priest at the Great Minster in 1519, led the first Reformed Reformation, making it a fountainhead of the Reformed (as distinct from the Lutheran) tradition. Zwingli began not with a theological crisis like Luther's but with the preaching of Scripture: he set aside the prescribed lectionary and preached straight through the books of the Bible, beginning with Matthew, and from that exposition of the Word the reform of Zurich flowed. Under his leadership and the city council's, the Mass was abolished, images and relics were removed from the churches, monasticism was ended, and worship was reordered to the simplicity the Reformed read in Scripture. The dictionary honours Zurich as a witness to the formal principle of the Reformation: that Scripture alone is the rule of faith and worship, that the word of God is truth and a lamp unto the feet, and that the church is to prove all things and hold fast that which is good. The reform of Zurich embodied the conviction that what Scripture does not warrant in worship is not to be imposed—the seed of the regulative principle the Reformed tradition would develop. The dictionary notes, without idealizing, the tragedies of Zurich's reform: Zwingli's death in battle at Kappel in 1531, the failure to agree with Luther on the Supper at the Marburg Colloquy, and the harsh persecution of the Anabaptists who arose there seeking a believers' church and believers' baptism—a persecution the Baptist tradition remembers with sorrow. Yet Zurich stands as the cradle of the Reformed faith, where the recovered Word of God reformed a city.

📜 Webster 1828 Definition

The Swiss city where Zwingli led the first Reformed Reformation from 1519 by preaching straight through Scripture; a fountainhead of the Reformed tradition and the regulative principle, though marked by the Marburg failure and the persecution of the Anabaptists.

ZURICH, proper noun. The Swiss city where Zwingli led the first Reformed Reformation from 1519.

Zwingli reformed the city by preaching straight through the books of Scripture.

The Mass was abolished, images removed, and worship reordered to Scriptural simplicity.

A fountainhead of the Reformed tradition and the seed of the regulative principle.

Marked also by the Marburg failure and the persecution of the Anabaptists.

⚠️ Modern Corruption

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition; the shadows on Zurich's reform are the failure to agree with Luther at Marburg and the harsh persecution of the Anabaptists who sought a believers' church.

expand to see more

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is the formal principle of the Reformation: Scripture alone as the rule of faith and worship. Zurich's reform began with the simple, revolutionary act of preaching straight through the books of the Bible, and from that exposition of the Word flowed the abolition of the Mass, the removal of images, and the reordering of worship. The dictionary honours Zurich as the cradle of the Reformed tradition and a witness that the recovered Word of God is the engine of all true reformation: thy word is truth, and a lamp unto the feet.

Yet the dictionary does not idealize the reform. Zwingli and the Lutherans failed to agree on the Lord's Supper at the Marburg Colloquy, fracturing the Protestant cause; Zwingli himself died sword in hand at the battle of Kappel, a tangling of the gospel with the sword the dictionary notes with sorrow. Most painfully for the Baptist tradition, it was at Zurich that the first Anabaptists arose, seeking a church of believers and believers' baptism, and were harshly persecuted, some drowned. The dictionary honours the Reformed recovery of the Word at Zurich while mourning the persecution of those who, following the same Word, sought a regenerate church—a lesson that even a true reformation must be reformed further by Scripture.

🔗 Greek & Hebrew Roots

The Swiss city (German Zürich) on the lake of the same name; its Great Minster (Grossmünster) was Zwingli's pulpit and the birthplace of the Reformed Reformation.

Zürich, the German name of the Swiss city.

The Grossmünster (Great Minster), Zwingli's pulpit from 1519.

Huldrych Zwingli, the first of the Reformed Reformers.

The Marburg Colloquy (1529), where Zwingli and Luther failed to agree on the Supper.

Birthplace of the Anabaptist movement, harshly persecuted there.
